passages.t: ‘O God, be not silent’: a ring of enemies
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A song. A Psalm of Asaph” (verse 1). It is the last of the psalms of Asaph. It opens with a plea to a God who seems quiet. “O God, be not silent; be not speechless; be not still, O God” (verse 1).

Enemies are plotting. They say, “Come, let us erase them as a nation; may the name of Israel be remembered no more” (verse 4). The psalm lists them, people after people around Israel's borders: Edom, Moab, Ammon, the Philistines, Tyre, and even far-off Assyria (verses 6 to 8).

So the psalmist asks God to do again what he did in the days of the judges. “Do to them as You did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the River Kishon” (verse 9). He asks God to scatter them like chaff before the wind and chase them with a storm (verses 13 to 15).

But look at the last lines. “Cover their faces with shame, that they may seek Your name, O LORD” (verse 16). And the goal of it all: “May they know that You alone, whose name is the LORD, are Most High over all the earth” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
No single war in the Bible's history matches this list of enemies. Some readers connect it with a time in King Jehoshaphat's day when Moab, Ammon and others marched against Judah (2 Chronicles 20). Others think the list gathers all of Israel's old enemies into one picture, a ring of danger on every side. The psalm does not say.

The names in verses 9 to 11 come from the book of Judges. Sisera and Jabin were the Canaanite commander and king defeated in Deborah's day (Judges 4:2). Oreb and Zeeb, Zebah and Zalmunna, were leaders of Midian defeated by Gideon (Judges 7:25; 8:21). A hearer would know those stories. They were stories of a small, weak people saved when all seemed lost.

‘Tumbleweed’ and ‘chaff’ (verse 13) were sights every farmer knew. On the threshing floor, the wind blew the light husks away and left the grain.
passages.later:
Jesus said, “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). On the cross he prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Paul wrote that God “wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). Psalm 83's last lines lean the same way: shame, so that they may seek God's name.
passages.hard:
This is one of the cursing psalms, and the book page's part on them sets out how Christians read prayers like this one. These notes do not choose between those readings.

One thing needs saying plainly. The names in this psalm, Edom, the Ishmaelites, Moab, the Philistines and the rest, belong to that ancient world and its wars. They are not modern peoples or nations, and this psalm gives no one any ground for contempt or hatred toward any people living today. To use it that way would turn a prayer to God into a weapon against neighbours, which is the very thing the psalm's own ending refuses.
passages.asks:
When you feel surrounded, you may pray this psalm's first line: ‘O God, be not silent.’ It is honest to ask God to act.

But let its ending shape what you want. The psalmist does not finally ask that his enemies vanish. He asks that they come to know the LORD. Can you pray that for the people who stand against you?
